body.heading: Change is not the breach
paragraphs: The friend who once lived for late nights now rises at dawn with a toddler. The partner who loved the city now dreams of a garden. None of this is betrayal — it is biography. Relationships break not when people change, but when the change cannot be spoken about.
Expecting someone to stay identical so the relationship can stay comfortable is a quiet kind of unfairness, and it never works for long.

body.heading: Renegotiate out loud
paragraphs: Healthy relationships hold small treaty talks: “Saturdays look different for me now — what could our version be?” The question honours both the change and the bond. It assumes the relationship is worth redesigning rather than either freezing or discarding.
Some renegotiations produce a smaller, truer friendship: fewer meetings, deeper ones. A smaller true thing outlasts a larger performed one.

body.heading: Grieve the old version honestly
paragraphs: Sometimes the renegotiation fails, and what remains is grief for a version of a person, and of yourself, that no longer exists. That grief is legitimate and does not need to be disguised as anger to be allowed.
People grow together, and people grow apart, and most long lives contain generous amounts of both. The art is telling which is happening while there is still time to choose your response with grace.

takeaway: Treat change as biography, renegotiate the relationship out loud, and grieve the old versions honestly when they pass.
